task.goal: Teach beginner spreadsheet users why sorting one column can detach values from their original rows.
hard_constraints: Use a fabricated eight-row table with no personal or financial data.
Some learners have only paper, so the core exercise must work without a computer.
Within 30 minutes, assess whether learners can detect and repair a broken association, not merely repeat a rule.
task.available_resources: Printed sample table, scissors, sticky notes and one optional projected spreadsheet.
task.expected_result: A hands-on explanation and a falsifiable learning check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Move the pieces: loose columns versus intact rows
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: make row associations physically visible, then show how independent movement destroys them. Each learner receives this fabricated eight-row table, with columns Token | Shape | Colour: A | circle | red; B | square | blue; C | triangle | green; D | star | yellow; E | oval | purple; F | diamond | orange; G | crescent | grey; H | hexagon | pink. Explain that each row describes one invented game piece.

In 0–5 minutes, learners inspect the table and retain an uncut reference. In 5–12 minutes, cut a second copy into three vertical column strips, then cut the Shape strip into eight cells. Alphabetize only those cells beside the unchanged Token and Colour columns. Ask learners to identify a token whose description has changed and explain what moved. In 12–18 minutes, reconstruct the original table using the reference, then cut it horizontally and alphabetize by Shape while moving whole rows. Compare the resulting associations.

What changes the outcome is the unit being moved: one attribute versus the complete record. Scissors and two printed copies per learner or pair suffice; sticky notes can hold loose cells. Projection is optional. This assumes learners can alphabetize the shape names; supply the alphabetical order if necessary. The reference is essential for reliable repair because the broken table alone generally cannot reveal the original pairings.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use minutes 18–27 for an individual check with the same eight records in a different starting order. Supply an intact reference and a version where only Colour was alphabetized; do not label which operation caused it. Require learners to identify two incorrect associations, restore all eight records, and produce a Shape-sorted table that preserves every association. Score these actions separately from any spoken rule. For a small comparison, give another group the same time with a verbal 'sort whole rows' explanation instead of the cutting exercise. The proposed benefit is unsupported if the hands-on group shows no better detection and repair; a small class can expose failure but cannot establish a reliable effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use a packing specification to audit and rebuild records
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: treat rows as claims that can be checked against an independent specification. Learners discover that a tidy, alphabetized column can still describe the wrong objects.

Print this fabricated eight-row table, with columns Kit | Tile | Mark: K1 | circle | dot; K2 | square | stripe; K3 | triangle | cross; K4 | star | ring; K5 | oval | wave; K6 | diamond | zigzag; K7 | crescent | grid; K8 | hexagon | spiral. Also print eight specification cards, each stating one complete kit description. These cards are the authoritative record, not clues inferred from appearance.

In minutes 0–5, explain that the table is a packing list for imaginary kits. In 5–12, hand learners a version with Tile alphabetized independently while Kit and Mark remain fixed. Ask them to inspect whether each listed kit would match its specification, using sticky notes to mark discrepancies. In 12–19, learners use the cards to rebuild the table and then arrange all eight complete records alphabetically by Tile. Ask why alphabetization did not establish correctness.

The outcome changes when learners check relationships against independent evidence rather than trusting a column's order. Implementation needs printed tables, specification cards, scissors and sticky notes. No computer is needed. This assumes learners can match kit labels and read the cards. It teaches recoverable errors: without an authoritative copy or another trustworthy relationship, original associations may be impossible to reconstruct.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In minutes 19–28, provide two unlabeled versions of the eight-row table: one correctly sorted by Tile, and one with only Mark sorted alphabetically. Let learners consult the specification cards. Individually, they must accept the valid version, identify two specific mismatches in the broken version, and repair all eight records. Include the valid version to catch indiscriminate claims that every reordered table is broken. Compare with a small group given the same cards and time but only the instruction 'always sort the entire table.' The mechanism is challenged if learners can recite that instruction yet cannot distinguish the versions or reconstruct the records, or if the audit activity offers no observable advantage over the simple instruction.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rewind the sort: recover associations from an action log
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: teach the error through reversible actions and their history. Learners repair a broken table by reversing recorded cell swaps, without consulting an intact answer copy. What changes the outcome is whether the reversal acts on the same cells that were originally moved.

Use this fabricated eight-row table, headed Robot | Signal: R1 | 4; R2 | 1; R3 | 7; R4 | 2; R5 | 8; R6 | 3; R7 | 6; R8 | 5. Each row describes an imaginary robot's signal number; neither column contains personal or financial data.

In minutes 0–5, establish that the signal belongs to the robot beside it. In minutes 5–13, pairs sort only Signal numerically by swapping two signal entries at a time, writing every pair of row positions on a paper action log. Sticky notes make entries movable; no computer is necessary. Require each swap to put the next smallest signal into its intended position, limiting the number of swaps. Learners then explain which robot descriptions changed and why an orderly column can contain incorrect associations.

In minutes 13–19, learners reverse the logged swaps, starting with the last entry. They then sort correctly by moving both entries of each row together. Emphasize that reversing a Signal-only operation requires another Signal-only operation; moving whole rows during repair would preserve the already broken pairings.

Needs: printed tables, paper logs and sticky notes. This assumes learners can follow numbered positions and reverse a short sequence; demonstrate one swap first. A complete, accurate log is essential. Sorting generally loses the previous order unless a reference, history or other trustworthy information survives. Whether this approach overloads beginners remains uncertain.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
In minutes 19–28, give each learner the eight records with Signal changed by three recorded swaps, without showing the intact table. Supply the chronological swap log, but no repair instructions. Require them to identify two affected robot associations, reconstruct their original signals using the history, and then sort the complete records by Signal. Prepare the answer key by independently reversing the supplied swaps.

Score detection, exact restoration of all eight pairings, and preservation during the final sort separately. Compare with learners receiving equal practice time and a simple explanation to sort whole rows, followed by the identical check and log. The proposed advantage is unsupported if the history exercise produces no better independent repair, or learners succeed only after being prompted to reverse the log. This small check can reveal failure; it cannot establish a reliable teaching effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use a built-in relationship to detect and repair mismatched rows
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: use a known relationship between two attributes as an error detector. Learners can reconstruct associations from that relationship without an intact reference or action history.

Print this fabricated eight-row table, headed Machine | Input | Output: M1 | 6 | 3; M2 | 2 | 7; M3 | 8 | 1; M4 | 4 | 5; M5 | 1 | 8; M6 | 7 | 2; M7 | 3 | 6; M8 | 5 | 4. Explain that these imaginary machines obey a design requirement: Input plus Output equals nine. Machine and Input are known to be unchanged; only Output may have moved.

During minutes 0–5, learners verify the requirement. During minutes 5–12, they write Output values on sticky notes and sort only those values into ascending order. They check each row again and mark violations. Ask why all the original numbers remain present while the descriptions have become incorrect. Position originally connected each output to its machine; moving outputs independently changed those connections.

During minutes 12–19, learners repair Output by finding the unique complement of each Input. They then sort by Output while moving complete rows, and verify the requirement again.

What changes the outcome is retained redundancy: the design requirement supplies enough information to recover the displaced values. Materials are one printed table and eight sticky notes per learner; scissors can create complete row strips. No computer is needed. Prerequisites are addition to nine and matching numbers; a printed complement guide can support arithmetic. The recovery works only because the requirement is trustworthy, Input is intact, and complements are unique. Most spreadsheets do not contain enough redundancy for this repair.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
During minutes 19–28, individually give learners two new arrangements of these eight records: one valid whole-row sort and one with Output independently sorted. Supply the design requirement and identify Input as intact, but give no repair procedure. Require learners to classify both tables, identify two specific broken associations, repair every output, and explain why moving complete rows of the broken table would preserve its errors.

Predeclare success as correct classification, eight restored associations, and an explanation identifying independent column movement. Compare with learners given equal time, the same requirement and materials, and a simple explanation plus ordinary whole-row sorting practice. The proposed exercise has no demonstrated advantage if it produces no better independent detection and repair. Correct arithmetic alone does not establish understanding; the explanation and valid-table classification are necessary checks. No results are assumed.

EXPAND.title: Rewind the operation to recover the relationships
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: teach sorting as a reversible movement whose history can restore associations. Recovery comes from reversing recorded movements, rather than matching against a correct copy.

Print this fabricated eight-row table, with columns Piece | Shape | Symbol: A | star | dot; B | circle | wave; C | triangle | ring; D | square | cross; E | oval | stripe; F | diamond | spiral; G | hexagon | grid; H | crescent | zigzag. Each row describes an imaginary piece.

Minutes 0–4: explain that a cell's row position determines which piece it describes. Minutes 4–11: learners cut only the Shape column into cells. To alphabetize it, follow a printed movement log: swap positions 1 and 2; swap 2 and 8; swap 3 and 6; swap 4 and 7; swap 6 and 7. After every swap, predict which pieces have acquired different shapes. This makes the causal chain explicit: moving a value changes its row partners.

Minutes 11–17: cover the original table. Ask learners to restore the associations by reading the log backward and reversing each swap. Then explain that spreadsheet Undo can similarly restore an immediately preceding mistaken sort, although available history depends on the application and session. Stop editing before attempting recovery; without trustworthy history or a saved reference, guessing is inappropriate.

Resources are printed tables and logs, scissors, and sticky notes for positional labels. Projection is optional. Learners must distinguish fixed row positions from moving values; supply numbered slots. This route assumes a complete, accurate movement history and does not promise recovery from an unknown sort.
EXPAND.experiment:
Minutes 17–28: individually give learners a fresh copy broken by three recorded swaps in Symbol, without an intact reference. Require two specific mismatches, reversal of all three swaps, and eight restored associations. The instructor retains the answer key. In a second short item, ask which cells must move together to sort by Shape safely.

For a first trial, the instructor compares this route with the prior intact-row cutting exercise, using equal instruction time and the same assessment. Record complete detection-and-repair success, completion time, and mistakes caused by reading the log forward. Stop adopting the extra logging procedure if success is no higher or additional tracking errors offset any gain. A small trial can reveal failure; it cannot establish a reliable general advantage.

EXPAND.title: Decide whether the evidence permits repair
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: make recoverability itself a judgment task. Learners distinguish detecting a broken association from knowing how to restore it, reducing confident but invented repairs.

Use this fabricated eight-row table, with columns Token | Form | Pattern: A | circle | dots; B | square | stripes; C | triangle | checks; D | star | waves; E | oval | rings; F | diamond | grid; G | crescent | plain; H | hexagon | spirals. These are imaginary tiles. Print an instructor master and separate case sheets derived from these same eight records.

Minutes 0–5: show how sorting Form alone leaves Token and Pattern in place, assigning forms to different tokens. Minutes 5–12: present two otherwise identical broken tables. Both carry a reliable note saying Form alone was sorted. Case A includes a verified original copy; Case B has neither a copy nor available undo history. Learners choose an action and justify it. In A, repair using the copy. In B, mark the affected associations as uncertain and request the original from the instructor acting as file owner. The note establishes that corruption occurred, but does not reveal the original pairings.

Minutes 12–18: show two different possible original Form arrangements that could yield the same alphabetized column. This demonstrates why alphabetic neatness cannot identify the lost relationships. Once the owner supplies the verified master, learners repair Case B.

Resources are printed sheets and sticky notes; scissors and projection are optional. The decision boundary is access to trustworthy recovery evidence, not confidence or visual plausibility. This assumes the instructor can supply a verified source after a justified request. Without one, the correct endpoint is an explicitly unresolved table.
EXPAND.experiment:
Minutes 18–29: individually assess the close pair above plus an unfamiliar case where only Pattern was sorted and an alleged backup contains just Token and Form. Require learners to choose repair or handoff, identify two affected associations when evidence permits, and restore all eight records after receiving the verified source. The unfamiliar backup cannot establish Pattern pairings, so immediate reconstruction is unjustified.

The instructor compares this route with the prior specification-card audit, giving both groups the same cases and access to the owner on request. Score correct decisions and complete repairs, plus unnecessary handoffs in the fully recoverable case and fabricated repairs in evidence-poor cases. Stop using the added decision exercise if it produces no improvement in justified recovery or increases unnecessary handoffs without reducing fabricated repairs. Results remain uncertain until tried; the added reasoning may consume time beginners need for actual reconstruction.

EXPAND.title: Move whole records, then verify by identity rather than position
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “Move the pieces: loose columns versus intact rows,” selected for its direct physical demonstration and low equipment burden. Changed action: after repair and whole-row sorting, learners verify associations by matching stable tokens against a differently ordered reference. This closes a consequential gap: beginners may mistake changed row positions for changed records, or copy reference positions instead of checking relationships.

Use this fabricated eight-row table, Token | Shape | Colour: A | circle | red; B | square | blue; C | triangle | green; D | star | yellow; E | oval | purple; F | diamond | orange; G | crescent | grey; H | hexagon | pink. Each row describes an imaginary tile.

Minutes 0–4: retain an uncut reference, arranged H through A, and explain that Token identifies a tile wherever its row appears. Minutes 4–11: cut a second copy into columns, cut Shape into cells, and alphabetize Shape alone beside the stationary columns. Learners name two tokens whose descriptions changed. Supply alphabetical order when needed. Minutes 11–16: each learner owns the repair: find each token in the reference and restore its Shape while leaving the other columns in place. Minutes 16–20: cut the repaired table into complete rows and sort by Shape. Partners verify all eight records by token, not by matching line numbers. If verification fails, return to the reference before continuing.

Resources: two printed copies per pair, scissors and sticky notes; projection is optional. If a cell is lost, the instructor supplies a replacement on a sticky note using the reference. If the reference is unavailable or incomplete, preserve the pieces and obtain the instructor master rather than guess. Reliable repair requires trustworthy original associations. The extra identity check takes time, but may prevent false alarms about legitimate sorting; its benefit is untested.
EXPAND.experiment:
Minutes 20–29: give each learner the same eight records in two unfamiliar row orders: one correctly sorted by Colour, the other with Shape alone alphabetized. Provide the reverse-order reference. Individually require acceptance of the valid table, two token-specific mismatches in the broken table, repair of all eight associations, and a Shape-sorted result preserving every complete record. Score detection, false alarms, complete repair and safe sorting separately.

The instructor runs a first trial against the source exercise with equal total time. Record completion time and requests for help as shifted costs. Retain the added identity check only if learners can finish within 30 minutes and it reduces position-based errors without lowering complete-repair success. Otherwise return to the simpler source exercise and revise the identity explanation. A small trial can reveal practical failure; it cannot establish general superiority.

EXPAND.title: Rebuild a meaningful value instead of retrieving an original
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: use a relationship learners can recompute from the surviving row contents. Previous routes depend on original records, specifications or movement history; here the table itself contains enough meaning to reconstruct the damaged attribute.

Print this fabricated eight-row table, Tile | Printed marks | Count: A | ***** | 5; B | ** | 2; C | ******** | 8; D | * | 1; E | ****** | 6; F | *** | 3; G | ******* | 7; H | **** | 4. Explain that Count means the number of stars printed for that imaginary tile. Space the stars clearly on paper. This deliberate redundancy makes the associations independently testable.

Minutes 0–5: learners count two rows and explain the relationship. Minutes 5–11: cut Count into individual cells and arrange it from 1 through 8 while Tile and Printed marks stay fixed. Ask whether the now orderly table still makes true statements. Minutes 11–17: learners detect contradictions by counting and repair Count using the marks in each row. No original copy is needed. Minutes 17–20: cut complete rows and sort them by Count; recount to show why this movement preserves truth.

Each learner owns counting and repair; the instructor resolves ambiguous printing by consulting the master. The decision boundary is explicit: recomputation is justified only because Printed marks is known to be intact and Count has a defined meaning. If marks are missing or unclear, stop reconstructing that row and request a legible instructor copy. Use sticky notes for replacement counts. Resources are printed tables, scissors and sticky notes; no computer is required.

This removes a recovery dependency for this exercise, not for arbitrary spreadsheet data. Shape names or colours usually cannot be reconstructed this way. Compared with reference-based repair, it avoids repeated lookups but adds counting effort and possible counting mistakes. No advantage is established yet.
EXPAND.experiment:
Minutes 20–29: the instructor gives each learner a fresh eight-row version using the same tiles and mark strings in a different order, with three changed Count cells, plus a correctly whole-row-sorted version. Learners must accept the valid version, identify the three contradictions, repair all eight associations, and explain using one row why moving Count alone caused an error. Score exact detection, complete repair and false alarms; retain an instructor answer key.

For a bounded first trial, compare this lesson with the simple instruction “sort complete rows” followed by equal paper practice and the same assessment. Record success, completion time and counting errors. Stop using the counting route if learners cannot finish within 30 minutes or counting errors erase any detection-and-repair benefit. Also ask whether an arbitrary lost colour could be recovered without a reference; treating counting as a universal recovery method is a failure requiring an explicit correction. Results remain uncertain until tried.
